rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify poorly resolved pairs while limiting run time. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the crowded central peaks respond to reduced steepness. The current last peak at 7.16 min leaves room to improve resolution while likely keeping all peaks within 10 min.

The limiting pair improved strongly with a shallower gradient, so narrow the solvent window to reduce steepness further. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset some added retention, targeting full resolution with the last peak still within 10 min.

Narrow the gradient window again to push the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. Increasing phi0 should help keep the last peak below 10 min, while the early peaks have ample separation to tolerate the stronger start.
Injection 4 already achieved the maximum CRF. Increase temperature by 5 C to seek a shorter fully resolved run, retaining injection 4 as the benchmark if the critical pair loses resolution.

Return to the temperature that achieved full resolution and preserve its gradient slope while shifting the starting organic fraction upward. This should shorten elution times; the run will test whether the early peaks and critical central pair retain adequate resolution.

The maximum CRF is already secured by injection 4, so test a higher-temperature selectivity regime for a shorter alternative. Moving beyond the near-coelution at 45 C may separate the critical pair after an elution-order reversal, though other pairs must also be checked.

Lower the starting organic fraction to retain and separate the early pair while preserving gradient steepness. This also tests whether the additional initial retention improves the crowded middle pair, with sufficient time margin to keep the last peak below 10 min.

Keep the weaker start that resolved the early pair and reduce temperature to shift the nearly coeluting middle pair. This intermediate temperature may resolve both central clusters while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 min.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness at 55 C to try to lift the remaining R = 1.41 pair above 1.5. Monitor the other central pair at R = 1.74, since changing slope could improve one pair at the expense of the other.

Test a weaker start combined with a steeper gradient at 55 C to seek faster elution without losing full resolution. The weaker start may improve middle-pair selectivity enough to offset gradient compression, while preserving the already adequate early separation.

Shorten only the gradient to seek a faster method matching the maximum CRF. The middle pair at R = 1.97 has room for compression, while the tighter pair may benefit slightly from increased steepness based on injections 9 and 10.

Reduce the gradient endpoint by one grid step to recover the small resolution deficit at R = 1.47. This modest slope reduction should retain most of injection 12's time savings while targeting full resolution.

Test a weaker start with a steeper gradient to seek a fully resolved run shorter than 8 min. The weaker start may preserve separation of the slope-sensitive middle pair, while the steeper gradient should help the other close pair and accelerate late elution.

With maximum CRF secured, test a substantially faster high-temperature gradient. At 60 C, increased steepness may separate the middle pair on the opposite side of its selectivity crossover, while the 0.15 start should retain adequate early-pair separation.

Test a cooler selectivity regime for a faster fully resolved alternative to injection 14. Cooling may separate the central cluster after another order reversal; the broad, relatively steep gradient should limit the added retention.

Test 35 C with a moderately shallower gradient to determine whether a useful selectivity window lies between the crowded 30 C pattern and the successful 40 C regime. The last peak should remain below 10 min, allowing resolution gains without a time penalty.

Test whether further steepening at 60 C improves the middle pair that reached R = 0.98 in injection 15. This targets a much shorter alternative, but the neighboring pair at R = 1.62 may become limiting; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Return to the fastest confirmed fully resolved selectivity regime and test a modestly steeper gradient. This probes whether the weaker start can preserve both critical pairs while reducing the last-peak time below injection 14's 7.60 min.

Preserve injection 14's starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while trimming the endpoint above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.57. This should reproduce its maximum CRF and 7.60 min last-peak time with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a gradient slope between injections 12 and 13, targeting full resolution with a last-peak time near 7.8 min. This may provide a slightly larger minimum-resolution margin than injection 20 while retaining most of its speed.

Probe the untested 50 C selectivity regime with a faster gradient. This may separate the central cluster after its near-coelution at 45 C, while the weaker starting composition should preserve early-pair resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction while preserving injection 22's gradient slope to test initial-composition selectivity for its limiting pair. This should shorten the run further, though both the early pair and the central cluster must retain R ≥ 1.5.

Trim injection 13's gradient while preserving its starting composition and slope, targeting its confirmed CRF of 1.000 and minimum resolution of 1.58. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Use the final injection to test a gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 14 and the faster but underresolved injection 19. This probes the speed–resolution boundary; injection 20 remains the shortest-gradient confirmed method attaining the maximum CRF.
